meta.topic: Chance that a parcel left unattended at a home's door is stolen, by market
meta.method: Publisher pages read with WebFetch where reachable; PDFs downloaded and text-extracted with pdftotext. confirmed:true only when the figure was read on the publisher's own page or document. Ofcom (ofcom.org.uk) returned HTTP 403 / a Cloudflare challenge to every fetch, so its figures are recorded from search-result summaries as confirmed:false.
caveats: No market publishes a per-parcel theft rate, and no carrier, regulator or survey found publishes the share of parcels left unattended. Every per-parcel figure below is a derivation, and divides thefts by ALL parcels, not by parcels left unattended.

Because thefts happen almost entirely to parcels left unattended, the true chance per unattended parcel = (thefts / all parcels) / (share of parcels left unattended). That share is < 1 and unpublished, so each derived figure is a FLOOR for the per-unattended-parcel chance, not the figure itself.

Theft surveys disagree by a factor of ~6 in the US (37M to 228M packages a year). They are commissioned by security/e-commerce vendors, online, and self-reported; 'stolen' is not separated from 'lost' or 'not delivered' in most of them.

Parcel volumes (Pitney Bowes, Ofcom) count all parcels generated, including business-to-business and returns, so a per-household-delivery denominator would be smaller and the per-parcel chance higher.

theftSurveys.methodQuote: In October 2025, Security.org polled 3,307 American adults about their personal experiences with package theft. The poll was conducted online. Participants' responses were weighted to be representative of the age, sex, and ethnicity of the U.S. population according to the Census.

theftSurveys.title: 2025 U.S. Package Theft Report and Worst Metro Cities for Porch Pirates
theftSurveys.method: 20-question online survey fielded August 2025 via Pollfish (Random Device Engagement), 50 respondents per state.
theftSurveys.note: The page as read describes the 2,500 as respondents who experienced package theft, which sits awkwardly with a 31% incidence figure; the sampling frame is unclear. No holiday or empty-home breakdown.

theftSurveys.title: U.S. Porch Piracy Report 2025
theftSurveys.method: Blend of FBI state residential-larceny data adjusted for under-reporting (25% weight) and a nationally representative CINT online survey of 1,000 US adults, margin of error 3% (75% weight).
theftSurveys.note: Highest US estimate by far. 1.8 thefts per 'average household' is not reconcilable with 29.7% incidence and 228M packages without knowing their household count; treat as an outlier.

theftSurveys.title: Package Theft in the United States, Report RISC-WP-25-002

figures.quote: With at least 58 million packages stolen in 2024 ... There is no single authoritative source for package theft data, and surveys vary in estimating the volume and costs associated with package theft.

theftSurveys.note: A federal review of the vendor surveys, not a survey itself. The 58M is Security.org's 2024 estimate. It also cites a 2018 Nextdoor member survey (2,000 members, May 2018) in which 62% had experienced package theft, a self-selected sample.

theftSurveys.title: Parcel theft research 2025 ('porch pirates strike every seven seconds')

figures.rateQuote: one package stolen every seven seconds

theftSurveys.note: Quadient's own page gives no sample or method. Trade-press reports (Commercial Motor, Motor Transport, retailrewired.co.uk, Nov 2025; not readable / secondary) add: one in six UK households affected; a 2,000-adult consumer survey; FOI responses from 27 of 45 police forces; police-recorded doorstep theft up 77%; 1,144 thefts reported to police in December 2024; 'nearly 60%' of thefts between 9am and 5pm 'when many homes are empty'. Those secondary figures are confirmed:false.

theftSurveys.title: New research reveals UK parcel theft hit £666.5m in the last year

figures.source: FOI responses from 27 of the UK's 45 police forces

theftSurveys.note: Secondary (a parcel-box vendor), consistent with Quadient. £666.5m / £138 = 4.83M parcels, matching 'one every seven seconds' (4.51M a year).

theftSurveys.title: Citizens Advice sounds the alarm on parcel delivery market as ten people have parcels lost or stolen per minute
theftSurveys.note: 'Lost or stolen' combined; sample not given in the release. Older than the Quadient figures.
No Irish parcel-theft incidence survey found (searched ComReg, An Post, news). ComReg's 2021 consumer research (doc 21/59) lists 'left outside' only as a reason for dissatisfaction.

No Mexican survey of doorstep parcel theft found. AMVO publishes online-fraud figures (e.g. 33% reported some online-shopping fraud in the prior two years, 2023) and Mexican press covers 'paquetes fantasma' and fake-courier scams, which are different crimes and must not stand in for doorstep theft.

leftUnattended.figure: Out-of-home deliveries (lockers, parcel shops) were 12% of measured parcel volumes in 2024-25
leftUnattended.note: Not a doorstep share: it only says 88% went to an address. The split of those 88% between handed over, neighbour, safe place and doorstep is not published.

leftUnattended.publisher: Citizens Advice (Opinium, 8,000 adults, 29 Aug-27 Sep 2025, released 19 Nov 2025)
leftUnattended.figure: 37% had a problem with their most recent delivery; among the problems, 'parcel being left in an insecure location (24%)' and 'driver leaving before they had time to get to the door (29%)'
leftUnattended.derivation: 0.37 x 0.24 = 0.0888, IF the 24% is of those with a problem. The release's wording leaves the base ambiguous; if the 24% is of all recipients, the share is 0.24.
leftUnattended.note: 'Insecure location' is the respondent's complaint, a subset of all unattended drops; consented safe places are not counted.

leftUnattended.figure: Being handed the package at the front door is the most common way to receive parcels in the US, UK and Germany; automated parcel stations used in the past 12 months by 11% (US), 17% (UK); parcel shop/post office 17-26%
leftUnattended.note: The chart page gives no number for 'left at the door' and no sample; it measures people who used a method in 12 months, not a share of parcels.

derived.formula: packagesStolenPerYear / deliveriesPerYear (floor for per-unattended-parcel chance; divide by the unpublished unattended share for the true figure)
derived.note: Low estimate: 37M / 22.0bn = 0.168% per delivered parcel. Same publisher for numerator and denominator, so the most internally consistent US figure. Mid estimate: SafeWise 104.3M / Pitney Bowes 23.1bn = 0.452%. High estimate: Omnisend 228M / 23.1bn = 0.987%. Recommended central value 0.168% to 0.452%; Omnisend's is an outlier.
Upper bound; method blends FBI larceny data with a 1,000-person survey.

derived.formula: Holiday multiplier = (share of thefts in Nov-Dec / share of parcels in Nov-Dec)

inputs.parcelShareNovDec: not published as a two-month figure; Security.org gives only Oct-Dec = 2x an average quarter

derived.note: Not computed: the parcel share for November-December alone is not published. If Oct-Dec carries 2/5 of the year's parcels (25 of ~62.5, Security.org) that is a three-month window and cannot be divided into a two-month theft share without inventing an input.

derived.formula: parcelsStolenPerYear / measuredParcelsPerYear, where parcelsStolenPerYear = seconds per year / 7
derived.note: 4.505M / 4.2bn = 0.107%. Removing Ofcom's 12% out-of-home volume (never left at a door): 4.505M / (4.2bn x 0.88 = 3.696bn) = 0.122%. Using 4.83M (iParcelBox: £666.5m / £138) gives 0.115% and 0.131%. Floor, as above.
Per parcel delivered to an address. Still a floor for per-unattended parcel, since most address deliveries are handed over or left with a neighbour.

derived.formula: shareOfPeopleWithTheftPerYear x theftsPerVictim / parcelsPerPerson, with theftsPerVictim set to 1 (minimum)

inputs.theftsPerVictim: not published for Canada; 1 used as the minimum, not as an estimate

derived.note: Rough and weak: 0.10 / 34 = 0.294%. Years differ (2024 survey, 2022 volume), the survey base is adults while parcels per person is over the whole population, and one household theft may be reported by several adults. No Canadian count of stolen packages exists to do this properly.
